Advowson
ad-VOW-zon
n. (the right of presenting a clergyman to a vacant parish benefice; in English law a property right, which could be inherited, granted or sold)
Anglo-French avoeson, from Latin advocatio, a calling to, from advocare, to summon or call in; the patron was the advocatus of the church.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

An advowson is the right to name the minister of a parish. In English law it was real property: it descended with a manor, could be sold apart from the land, could be mortgaged, and was litigated in the royal courts. Monasteries accumulated advowsons in hundreds, because the right to present carried with it the power to appropriate the tithes and leave a poorly paid vicar in charge. The arrangement survived the Reformation and parts of it survive still. The New Testament says nothing about such a right and a good deal about the appointment of ministers, and the pattern is uniformly ecclesiastical rather than proprietary. “when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord” (Act 14:23). Titus is left in Crete to “ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5) by a stated standard of character. And the final appointment is not in human hands at all: “the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines advowson as a right of presentation to a church or ecclesiastical benefice; and patron as one who has the gift of a benefice, one who protects or supports.

expand to see more

ADVOWSON, n. In English law, a right of presentation to a church or ecclesiastical benefice. Advowson signifies taking into protection, and is synonymous with patronage.

PATRON, n. In the church of England and of Rome, one who has the gift and disposition of a benefice; a protector; a defender.

PRESENT, v.t. To nominate to an ecclesiastical benefice; to offer to the bishop or ordinary as a candidate for institution.

BENEFICE, n. In the middle ages, benefice was used for a fee. In church affairs, an ecclesiastical living; a church endowed with a revenue.

INDUCTION, n. In ecclesiastical affairs, the giving a clerk possession of a benefice, after institution.

Key Scripture

Act 14:23 — "And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed."

Tit 1:5 — "For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:"

Act 20:28 — "Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood."

Tit 1:7 — "For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre;"

Modern Corruption

The right to name a parish's minister, held as property and sold like land.

expand to see more

The corruption is the ownership of a pulpit. Once the right to present is property, the man presented is chosen by whoever holds the deed, for whatever reasons property owners have; younger sons were placed in livings they never visited, and the congregation had no voice in either case. It is not simony, because the office itself was not sold, only the right to fill it — a distinction the law maintained carefully and the sheep could not detect.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the qualifications for the ministry are stated and testable, and that they are about the man: “For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre” (Tit 1:7). Where a church cannot examine a man against that list before he is set over it, the list is a dead letter whatever is written in the parish register.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin advocatio, a calling in; Greek cheirotoneo (G5500), to appoint or ordain; Greek kathistemi (G2525), to set in place; Greek episkopos (G1985), an overseer; Greek peripoieomai (G4046), to purchase.

expand to see more

Latin advocare — to call in; the patron as the church's advocatus.

Greek cheirotoneo (G5500) — to appoint, to ordain; “when they had ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23).

Greek kathistemi (G2525) — to appoint, to set in office; “and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5).

Greek episkopos (G1985) — an overseer; “the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers” (Act 20:28).

Greek peripoieomai (G4046) — to acquire, to purchase; “which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28).

Usage

"“and had prayed with fasting” (Act 14:23) — how the apostolic church filled a vacancy."

"“as the steward of God” (Tit 1:7) — the man is a steward, not a tenant."

"“Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28) — the charge no deed conveys."
